newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end quiet session higher.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end quiet session higher.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended higher on Friday, a day devoid of fresh economic news.
"It was a really quiet day," said William Hornbarger, fixed-income strategist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc.
The 30-year Treasury bond ended at 99-26/32, up 6/32 to yield 6.64 percent, and stayed within a quarter-point range throughout the trading session.
Just passing attention was paid to remarks by Federal Reserve Vice-Chairman Alice Rivlin and Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan on Friday.
Rivlin said recent U.S. wage growth had not sparked inflation yet because productivity appeared to be growing even faster. Fed Chairman Greenspan warned against overregulating derivatives.
But analysts said Friday's modest gains after three straight sessions of losses this week had ended the chapter of the bond market's most recent rally.
"This week marked the end of a rally that had clearly run out of steam," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc. "So it's a new ballgame now."

"From this point onward, we'll be taking our cues from new pieces of information like (Federal Reserve Chairman Alan) Greenspan's (Humphrey-Hawkins) testimony (on February 26-27) and after that, (the January) durable goods (report)," Karydakis said. "This is no longer a rally living on its own momentum. It's different now."
Analysts agreed that the market's focus had shifted to Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.
"Since the CPI was released on Wednesday, people have been waiting for the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony," said Joshua Feinman, vice president and economist at Bankers Trust.
"After that, attention will turn to the next employment report," he said. The February employment report is due on Friday, March 7.
"Everyone is very curious to hear the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony," agreed Hornbarger. "Then come the employment data.
"The one thing people are concerned about is the potential for wage inflation, so the (February) employment number looms rather large," Hornbarger said.
The market has also begun to trade on a when-issued basis the two- and five-year notes that the Treasury plans to auction on Tuesday and Wednesday, respectively.
Participants seemed quite sanguine about prospective demand for those securities.
"The two- and five-year auctions are monthly events," said Hornbarger. "The market rallied through the quarterly refunding so I don't think there will be any problem getting those done."

"I can't see too many people getting excited about the two's and the five's, but we won't get a repeat of the refunding phenomenon when the market rallied right through (some fairly disappointing auctions)," said Karydakis. "Supply will be a neutral factor next week."
In when-issued trade on Friday, the two-year notes ended with a 5.86 percent yield. The five-year Treasury notes to be auctioned on Wednesday ended with a 6.1625 percent yield.
At the short end of the maturity curve, three-month bill rates rose one basis point to 4.96 percent. Six-month and year-bill rates were unchanged at 5.02 percent and 5.18 percent, respectively.
Two-year notes ended unchanged at 100-2/32, yielding 5.84 percent. Five-year notes closed at 100-11/32, up 1/32, yielding 6.17 percent. Ten-year notes ended at 99-4/32, up 4/32 to yield 6.37 percent.
